clue.text: Miss return of travellers about this month

indicators.note: the turned word sits about, i.e. around, the abbreviation for this month
a return goes back the way it came, so the word for travellers is read backwards

parts.note: commercial travellers are sales reps
inst., short for instant, is the commercial-letter term for the current month

explanation.surface: A young woman awaits the return of salesmen sometime this month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a verb but is the title of an unmarried woman; 'return of' reads the travellers backwards and 'about' puts them round the month.
explanation.definitionFit: An unmarried woman is addressed as Miss, and an older single woman is traditionally called a spinster.

clue.text: Ironic address to one replacing a square

indicators.note: one thing replacing another means a letter of the word is swapped out for a new one

parts.note: taken as written: the word square itself
the letter named by the clue's own word a
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Advice on how to talk mockingly to someone who stands in for a stuffy conventional type.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech 'squire' is a mock-respectful way of addressing a man, as a market trader might ('What can I get you, squire?').
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a stranger by the old title for a country landowner is a jocular, faintly mocking form of address in Britain.

clue.text: Lodge in pub with worker up in arms

indicators.note: the lodging word goes inside the word for a pub

parts.note: an inn is a pub
to dig, or have digs, is to lodge in rented rooms
the worker ant is the crossword's standard worker

explanation.surface: Someone lodging above a pub alongside a labourer is furious about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lodge' reads as a noun in the surface but is the verb DIG (as in 'digs', lodgings).
explanation.definitionFit: Being up in arms is an idiom for being angrily resentful, the meaning of indignant.

clue.text: Take a walk to Mancunian ford, not quite straight horseflies about

parts.note: Stretford in Greater Manchester is named as the ford on the stret, the old Roman street, so the stret is that ford's first element

indicators.note: the horseflies word goes about, i.e. around, the shortened word for straight

parts.note: clegs is the British dialect name for horseflies

indicators.note: not quite the whole word means its final letter is cut off

parts.note: straight in the sense of truthful is honest

explanation.surface: A rambler sets off towards a ford near Manchester, swatting at the horseflies circling about.
explanation.walkthrough: Stretford is a district of Greater Manchester whose name means the ford on the Roman street; 'not quite' clips the last letter of straight, and 'about' puts the horseflies round what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Going for a stroll after sitting a long time is the idiom's sense, the same as taking a short walk.

clue.text: With clay so dry, common sense treatment is to take a walk

definitions.text: With clay so dry, common sense treatment is to take a walk

indicators.note: giving the letters a treatment works them over into a new order

explanation.surface: Advice that with parched clay underfoot, the sensible remedy is simply to go for a stroll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treatment' shuffles CLAY, SO, DRY, COMMON and SENSE (20 letters). Read whole, the clue also says the cure for the condition is walking about, which is the advice to long-haul fliers.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep-vein thrombosis from sitting cramped on long flights has this popular name, and the advice against it is to get up and move about the cabin.

clue.text: Counter where sailor takes a customer's part

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is the usual crossword sailor

indicators.note: a part of the word is taken, its opening letters

explanation.surface: A shop counter where a seaman takes a customer's side in a dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counter' looks like a shop counter but is a counting frame.
explanation.definitionFit: A frame of beads on wires is used for reckoning sums, so it is a device for counting.

clue.text: Striker to be involved with flirtation with death in the air

parts.note: a bat is something you strike a ball with

indicators.note: letters that are involved get tangled together into a new order

explanation.surface: A footballer who is to be caught up in a flirtation finds romance in the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striker' suggests a footballer but is the BAT; 'involved' mixes BE with FLIRTATION to make TLEOFBRITAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1940 air campaign over southern England cost thousands of airmen their lives, aerial warfare where death came from the sky.

clue.text: See 4
See 4
Spoil the setter to rouse the cat

parts.note: the setter of a crossword refers to themselves as me

indicators.note: rousing makes something rise, so in a down clue the word is turned upwards

parts.note: puss is a familiar name for the cat

explanation.surface: The crossword setter ruins things by waking the sleeping cat.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'to rouse' (make it get up) turns PUSS upward to SSUP.
explanation.definitionFit: To mess up is to bungle or ruin, so it means spoil.

clue.text: Formerly — could be any time, about — declared with restraint

indicators.note: the word for could be any time goes about, i.e. around, the word for formerly

parts.note: something undated could belong to any time
erst is an archaic word for formerly, as in erstwhile

explanation.surface: A remark once made, at some unknown time, was said only mildly.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes make 'could be any time' look like an aside, but it is the outer word, and 'about' wraps it round the archaic word for formerly.
explanation.definitionFit: Stating something in a deliberately restrained way is understating it.

clue.text: Cause staleness in athletes by evident precipitation

parts.note: overt means open and evident
rain is the commonest precipitation

explanation.surface: Athletes are going stale because of the obvious downpour.
explanation.definitionFit: Training too hard leaves sportsmen jaded and below their best, which is what overtraining means.

clue.text: Just rogues, hit for a change

indicators.note: putting letters through a change rearranges them into a different word

explanation.surface: Only villains get hit, just for a change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like 'only' but is the adjective meaning fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Being morally upright and fair is the sense shared by just and righteous.

clue.text: In the cathedral a service demands concentration

indicators.note: the letters sit in the run of words that follows, across their joins

explanation.surface: Attending a cathedral service requires focus.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is cathedraL A SERvice.
explanation.definitionFit: A laser beam is light concentrated into a narrow intense stream.

clue.text: China animal with fodder

parts.note: a cat is an animal
hay is dried grass used as fodder

explanation.surface: A ceramic animal sits beside its feed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like porcelain but is the old name for the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Cathay is the medieval European name for the country of China.

clue.text: It's difficult to take the French in the afternoon

indicators.note: the stealing word and the French article go inside the time abbreviation

parts.note: p.m., post meridiem, marks the afternoon
to rob is to take unlawfully
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Someone finds it hard to bring French food in the afternoon.
explanation.definitionFit: A difficulty or matter hard to solve is a problem.

clue.text: Walker sailed off, being now permitted…

parts.note: a leg is what one walks with

indicators.note: off in the sense of gone wrong signals the letters going astray into a new order

explanation.surface: A rambler sailed away, now that it is allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walker' suggests a hiker but is a leg; 'off' scrambles sailed. The ellipsis leads on to 17, which asks whether that drug should be permitted.
explanation.definitionFit: Something made lawful by statute is allowed, so legalised means now permitted.

clue.text: Should this be so? Reverse ban, in dog Latin?

indicators.note: the turned word goes in the Latin word for dog

parts.note: canis is the Latin for dog

indicators.note: reverse tells us to read the word ban backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A query about whether a ban should be reversed, couched in mock Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: Following the ellipsis from 16, 'Should this be so?' asks whether this drug should be legalised. 'Reverse' turns ban round inside the Latin dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue asks whether this drug, the subject of the legalisation debate, ought to be made lawful.

clue.text: As friend to foe, the friend of Caesar, J.

explanation.surface: A tribute to the man who stood by Julius Caesar.
explanation.walkthrough: Caesar, J. is Julius Caesar written surname first; his friend Mark Antony written the same way is Antony, M.
explanation.definitionFit: Friend and foe are words of opposite meaning, an opposite-word pair; and Mark Antony written surname first with initial gives the same letters.

clue.text: Mate spreading manure?

explanation.surface: A pal who spreads dung on the fields.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a close pal is a mucker; and one who spreads muck, i.e. manure, would be a mucker too.

clue.text: Island part of country with holder in as well

indicators.note: the holder word goes in the word for as well

parts.note: too means as well
a bag holds things

explanation.surface: Part of an island nation also has a container inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobago is the smaller island of the Caribbean nation Trinidad and Tobago.

clue.text: Like a pipe in the bath? Turn to a household god

parts.note: a tub is a bath
a U-turn, so U stands for a turn
a lar was a Roman household god

explanation.surface: A pipe in the bathroom turns towards a domestic deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaped as a tube, a pipe is cylindrical and hollow.

clue.text: See 10
Fixers at one's fingertips

explanation.surface: Handymen with everything to hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Small metal pins hammered in are fixings; and the horny plates on the ends of one's fingers are found right at the fingertips.

clue.text: Flag for Hungary or Hibernian

parts.note: the flag is the yellow iris plant
H is the international vehicle code for Hungary

explanation.surface: Choosing a banner either for Hungary or for an Irish team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' looks like a national banner but is the plant. Hibernian is from Hibernia, the Latin name for Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Hibernia was the Roman name for Ireland, so Hibernian is a literary word for Irish.

clue.text: Carriage supplies shelter retained by old humanist

indicators.note: one word is retained, held inside, by the other

parts.note: John Colet was a Tudor humanist scholar, founder of St Paul's School
an abri is a shelter, especially a dugout

explanation.surface: A horse-drawn coach provides cover, protected by a Renaissance scholar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retained by' puts the shelter word, a French borrowing used in English for a dugout, inside the name of the Tudor scholar.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabriolet was a light two-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle, and the word now names a convertible car.

clue.text: Correction here: groom OK too?

explanation.surface: At a wedding, after a check on the bridegroom, someone asks if all is fine.
explanation.walkthrough: A bridewell is an old house of correction, named after the London prison. The second reading: if the groom is OK, is the bride well too?
explanation.definitionFit: A bridewell was a prison or house of correction; and asking whether the groom's partner is in good health too gives bride well.

clue.text: Advantage in the arranged manner

parts.note: as means in the manner of, so in the ... manner gives as
set means arranged, as in set out

explanation.surface: Being able to do things the planned way is a plus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the arranged manner' is 'as set'.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is something useful or valuable, a benefit.

clue.text: Division — schoolmaster is included

indicators.note: one word is included inside the other

parts.note: Sch. is short for school and M for master
taken as written

explanation.surface: Discord in the staffroom: the head teacher is caught up in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'included' puts is inside the abbreviations for school and master run together.
explanation.definitionFit: A split in a group, especially a church, is a schism.

clue.text: Island part of country among instincts in the square

indicators.note: the two short words go in the word for square

parts.note: trad, short for traditional, means old-fashioned or square
in can mean among
the id is the instinctive part of the psyche in Freud

explanation.surface: Part of an island nation sits among gut feelings in the town square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'square' looks like a town square but means old-fashioned, TRAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Trinidad is the larger island of the Caribbean nation Trinidad and Tobago.
